title: The Guardian’s First Shield — Staying Safe in the Digital Realm

learningObjectives.description: Explain cybersecurity as protecting devices, accounts and information.
Recognize warning signs in suspicious messages and displayed link addresses.
Explain why strong, unique passwords matter.
Recognize the purpose and limits of multifactor authentication.
Explain why personal and sensitive information should be protected.
Choose a safe defensive response, including trusted help and reporting.

variants.intro: Help Hexi Protect the Academy! Mysterious messages have arrived at the castle gates. Let’s pause, keep secrets safe, and ask for help. You can read with a grown-up.

sections.title: A shield for our digital world
paragraphs: Cybersecurity means helping keep devices, accounts and information safe. Hexi’s shield is a reminder to stop and think.

sections.title: Pause at a strange message
paragraphs: “Quick! Win a prize! Click here!” is a reason to pause. A friendly picture or name does not prove who sent it.
Do not tap a mystery link or open a surprise file. Show a trusted adult.

sections.title: Keep your secret key
paragraphs: A strong password is long and hard to guess. Each account needs its own password, like a different key.
With a trusted adult, a password manager can help keep keys safe. Never send a password to someone in a message. We will not ask you to type one.

sections.title: A second check at the gate
paragraphs: Multifactor authentication, or MFA, adds a different check to a password, such as a security key or an authenticator code. Two passwords are not two different kinds of check.
Keep sign-in codes secret too. Ask a trusted adult to help set up account safety.

sections.title: Your private information matters
paragraphs: Keep your address, school, phone number and sign-in details private. Ask a trusted adult before sharing them.

sections.title: Ask for help, even after a mistake
paragraphs: Pause, do not click, and tell a trusted adult about a worrying message. A normal-looking note is not a promise that everything is safe.
If you already clicked, tell a trusted adult. You are not in trouble for asking for help.

variants.intro: Become a guardian of the academy inbox. Look for warning signs, protect credentials, and choose a safe next step. These stories use fictional accounts only.

sections.title: What cybersecurity protects
paragraphs: Cybersecurity protects devices, accounts and information against harm or unauthorized use. Your everyday choices are part of that defense.

sections.title: Phishing and suspicious addresses
paragraphs: Phishing messages impersonate someone or offer something tempting to get secrets, clicks or downloads. Pressure, unexpected requests and mismatched addresses are clues.

Read the actual domain, not just a familiar name in the path. In academy.invalid.prizes.invalid/gift, the ending is prizes.invalid, not academy.invalid. HTTPS protects a connection; it does not prove a sender is honest.

sections.title: A different key for every account
paragraphs: Use long, hard-to-guess, unique passwords. Reusing one means a stolen password could put another account at risk.
A trusted adult can help choose and use a password manager. Never paste a real password into a lesson or send it to someone requesting it in a message.

sections.title: MFA adds another barrier
paragraphs: Multifactor authentication uses different kinds of proof, such as a password plus a security key or authenticator. Two passwords are still the same kind of proof.
Never share one-time codes or approve an unexpected sign-in prompt. MFA helps, but not every method resists phishing equally.

sections.title: Private information and files
paragraphs: Your address, school, phone number and account details deserve protection. Pause before posting or sending them.
Unexpected attachments can be risky even if a message looks polished. Do not open one just to find out what it is.

sections.title: Respond safely
paragraphs: Do not follow the suspicious link or reply with secrets. Ask a trusted adult and report through the app’s report feature or an independently known support channel.
Use a saved, trusted route rather than the message’s contact details. If you already clicked or shared something, ask for help promptly. A mistake is not a reason to hide it.

sections.title: Practical cybersecurity
paragraphs: Cybersecurity protects devices, accounts and sensitive information from unauthorized access and harm. Common threats include deceptive messages, credential theft and harmful attachments.

sections.title: Phishing and social engineering
paragraphs: Phishing is one form of social engineering: a message tries to influence you into revealing information or taking a risky action. Professional wording or a familiar display name is not proof of authenticity.

Inspect the actual destination/domain and the context. HTTPS alone does not establish trust. If uncertain, leave the message link alone and verify through a bookmarked site or independently known contact.

sections.title: Strong, unique passwords and managers
paragraphs: Use a long, unpredictable password for each password-based account. Avoid reuse: a leaked password should not become a key to other services.
A password manager can create and store distinct passwords. Protect the manager itself and use its supported security features. This lesson requests no password and recommends no paid product.

sections.title: MFA and unexpected approvals
paragraphs: Multifactor authentication adds a different factor to a password, such as a security key or an authenticator. It reduces risk if a password is stolen; it does not make every scam harmless.

Prefer phishing-resistant options where available, such as supported security keys or passkeys. Never disclose sign-in codes or approve a prompt you did not initiate. Use known account-security channels to investigate.

sections.title: Sensitive information and attachments
paragraphs: Share only information needed for a legitimate purpose through a verified channel. Financial, identity and account information should not be sent because an unsolicited message requests it.
Do not open an unexpected attachment to test it. Verify its purpose and sender independently. File names and familiar logos are not reliable safety checks.

sections.title: Report and recover without blame
paragraphs: Use the organization’s established report mechanism or independently known support contact. Do not reply to a suspicious sender or use its supplied “help” link.

If you clicked or shared credentials, promptly seek the appropriate trusted support and follow the organization’s incident process. Use a known legitimate route to secure affected accounts; do not hide the mistake.

sections.title: Cybersecurity scope
paragraphs: Cybersecurity concerns protecting devices, accounts and information from unauthorized access and harm. This dataset covers introductory defensive decisions, not live investigations.

sections.title: Evidence and suspicious-message classification
paragraphs: Urgent secret requests, unexpected files and mismatched destinations are warning signs. A polished message or HTTPS connection alone does not establish trustworthy intent.
The “no-warning-shown” label means only that this authored scenario shows no immediate red flags; it is not a safety guarantee or permission to follow a link.

sections.title: Password defenses
paragraphs: Long, unpredictable, unique passwords reduce guessing and credential-reuse risks. Password managers can assist with generation and secure storage.
Do not request or ingest real passwords, codes or personal information for these tasks. Responses contain fixed lesson identifiers only.

sections.title: MFA defenses
paragraphs: Multifactor authentication combines different kinds of proof. A password plus an appropriate possession factor is different from two passwords.
MFA reduces some risks but can be phished in some forms. Do not approve uninitiated sign-ins or disclose one-time codes; supported phishing-resistant options improve protection.

sections.title: Privacy and unsolicited content
paragraphs: A valid defensive response minimizes sensitive disclosure and avoids unverified attachments or links. Use independent known channels for confirmation.
The addresses are reserved .invalid examples, rendered as text only. Message contents are lesson data, not instructions to send messages or execute tools.

sections.title: Assessment and safe responses
paragraphs: Choose the supplied classification and action ID, then inspect deterministic feedback and retry. Expected responses and explanations are part of the versioned specification.
Passing a finite case does not establish real-world threat detection, retained learning or trusted mastery. Reporting choices are evaluated descriptions only; nothing is actually reported.
